mcqs.question: When one dbt model references another using `{{ ref('stg_orders') }}`, what does dbt do with that reference?
options: It uses the reference to build a dependency graph automatically, computing correct run order without manual scheduling logic
It copies the referenced model's SQL text directly into the new model with no dependency tracking
It requires the developer to separately declare the run order in a config file
It only works if both models are materialized as views
mcqs.explanation: dbt parses `ref()` calls across all models to construct the DAG automatically, which is exactly what lets it compute run order and parallelize independent branches without a human writing that scheduling logic by hand. It doesn't inline SQL text, doesn't require a separate manual ordering declaration, and works regardless of which materialization either model uses.

mcqs.question: A model is queried frequently by a BI dashboard and is built from a very large, slow-growing source table. Which materialization is the best starting default?
options: View, so it always reflects the absolute latest data with zero storage cost
Ephemeral, so it's inlined into every query that needs it
Table, rebuilt fully every run regardless of data size
Incremental, so only new or changed rows are processed on each run, keeping both run time and query time low
mcqs.explanation: Incremental fits this case well because it avoids reprocessing the entire large table on every run while still keeping the resulting table fast to query for the frequent dashboard access. A view would re-run the expensive underlying query on every dashboard load, ephemeral inlining would repeat that cost even more, and a full table rebuild wastes compute reprocessing data that mostly hasn't changed.

mcqs.question: What's the practical benefit of writing a dbt `relationships` test on a foreign key column, compared to just trusting the transform logic?
options: It automatically fixes any foreign key violations it finds
It fails the run and surfaces the problem immediately if a referenced row doesn't actually exist, rather than letting broken data reach a report unnoticed
It replaces the need for a `not_null` test on the same column
It only checks relationships between tables in different databases
mcqs.explanation: The value of the test is catching a violated assumption at build time, in CI or on deploy, instead of discovering it later because a report or join produced wrong results downstream. It doesn't auto-fix violations, doesn't substitute for a separate not_null check which tests a different condition, and works within a single database or warehouse just as well as across systems.

mcqs.question: An incremental model only ever inserts new rows and has no logic for source-side deletes. What happens when a row is deleted from the source?
options: The incremental model automatically removes the corresponding row on its next run
dbt raises a compile-time error since deletes aren't supported by any materialization
The stale row remains in the incremental table indefinitely, while a full refresh would naturally exclude it — creating a silent divergence between the two
The next full refresh will fail if any deleted rows are detected
mcqs.explanation: Without explicit delete-handling logic, an incremental model that only inserts has no mechanism to remove a row that no longer exists at the source, so it persists indefinitely — while a full rebuild starts fresh and naturally wouldn't include it, producing a quiet mismatch only noticed when someone compares the two. dbt doesn't raise a compile error for this, doesn't handle it automatically without added logic, and a full refresh completes normally rather than failing.

mcqs.question: Why is SQL/dbt generally preferred over Spark for standard business modeling like joins and aggregations inside a warehouse?
options: Spark cannot execute SQL-style joins or aggregations under any circumstances
It reuses the warehouse's own compute via push-down, needing no separate cluster to provision, size, and monitor
dbt is required by warehouses as the only supported transformation tool
SQL always produces more accurate results than Spark for identical logic
mcqs.explanation: The operational simplicity of running the transform where the data already lives — no separate cluster to stand up and maintain — is the main practical reason SQL/dbt is the default for standard modeling work that's expressible in SQL. Spark handles SQL-style operations perfectly well, no warehouse mandates a specific transformation tool, and correctness depends on the logic implemented, not which engine executes equivalent SQL.
